claims.text: HEBM for 20–30 hours followed by SPS at 1100–1200 °C, 50–60 MPa, and 5–10 minutes will produce CoCrFeNiTi with greater than 99.5% relative density.
The proposed process will produce a nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi alloy with a grain size of 200–400 nm.
The resulting phase composition will be approximately 85% FCC, 15% BCC, and less than 1% HCP.
Rapid SPS heating and cooling will suppress diffusion-driven formation of brittle HCP and kinetically retain an FCC/BCC solid solution.
HCP in Ti-containing systems is stabilized by Ti segregation and oxygen or other interstitials.
Dual-phase stability is maximized at 1150 ± 50 °C with a heating rate greater than 100 °C/min.
An argon atmosphere containing less than 10 ppm oxygen and a sintering vacuum below 10^-3 Pa are required to prevent oxygen-induced HCP stabilization.
High-energy milling creates severe lattice defects and short-circuit diffusion paths that promote solid-solution formation.
SPS pressure suppresses porosity in the processed CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
A short SPS dwell prevents grain growth and oxide precipitation.
The processed alloy will have a dislocation density greater than 10^14 m^-2.
Fine grains provide Hall–Petch strengthening, while solute effects and high dislocation density also contribute to strength.
The processed alloy will exhibit a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV10.
The processed alloy will exhibit a compressive yield strength of 1200–1400 MPa and ductility greater than 10%.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi is porous, coarse-grained, single-phase FCC, and has hardness below 200 HV.
Oxygen contents above 0.5 wt% during milling will stabilize HCP and cause brittle fracture.
Sintering above 1300 °C may cause excessive grain growth or HCP formation.
SPS pressures below 30 MPa may leave residual porosity.
The proposed falsification experiment compares samples processed under less than 10 ppm oxygen and approximately 1000 ppm oxygen using a 9.8 N indentation load and a 15-second dwell.
Inadvertent oxygen uptake may raise hardness above 600 HV while causing embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The claimed kinetic-trapping regime requires a heating rate greater than 100 °C/min, but the specified intervention uses exactly 100 °C/min.
The experiment specifies a 9.8 N indentation load, corresponding to approximately HV1, while the reported measurement and prediction are labeled HV10, which conventionally uses a 98.1 N load.
The structural mediator asserts absence of HCP, whereas the predicted outcome permits a nonzero HCP fraction below 1%.
